newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Credit, EBR data to confirm Irish economic buoyancy.
newsitem.headline: Credit, EBR data to confirm Irish economic buoyancy.

text.p: Exchequer borrowing and credit data, due for release later this week, are expected to confirm the buoyancy of the Irish economy, analysts said on Monday.

End-June Exchequer borrowing data, due on Wednesday, should show a substantial surplus because of the strength of tax receipts while credit data for May are unlikely to show any marked slowdown in lending activity, they say.
Analysts forecasts for Exchequer borrowing range from a surplus of 100 million to 650 million Irish pounds compared with a borrowing requirement of 455 million in the same period last year.

"The main factor behind this impressive performance is greater-than-expected tax revenue buoyancy, reflecting the continued strong growth of the Irish economy," said AIB Group Treasury's bond unit, which forecasts a 650 million surplus.
Analysts note that last year's mid-June figure was affected by the late arrival of corporation tax receipts but say these should revert to their normal pattern this year.
"The numbers should be positive for the market, highlighting the need for only a limited issuance of fresh stock over the remainder of the year," said Alan McQuaid, economist at Bloxham Stockbrokers.
However, McQuaid noted that the direction of the market in the near-term is likely to be driven by overseas events.
Thursday's underlying credit growth data, due for release by the central bank, could show a slight slowdown in May as factors which boosted borrowing in March and April unwind, analysts said.
Forecasts for underlying credit growth range from 18.5 percent to 20.5 percent against 19.0 percent in April.
Credit growth jumped by 6.7 percent in March/April because of corporate borrowing to pay taxes in March and investor borrowing to short the Irish pound in April.
"For May, total borrowing should ease back on account of an easing in punt selling pressure," said Riada Stockbrokers who forecast underlying credit growth of 18.5 percent.
But Riada expect no signs of a slowdown in mortgage lending growth which is seen accelerating to 14.5 percent from 14.3 percent in March and April.
Analysts say borrowing to finance the purchase of Norwich Union shares should not have a major impact on the May credit data, showing up in the June figures instead.

The strength of underlying credit growth, which has accelerated from 11.5 percent year-on-year to 19 percent in the past year, is unlikely to allow any loosening of Irish monetary policy, analysts say.
"We expect credit growth to top in the coming months but remain at a high level," said AIB's bond unit. "This suggests that the Central Bank will be slow to unwind the recent hike in interest rates.
